subject: FINLY discovery recap: p95 latency & concurrency requirements
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Sam Patel <sam.patel@finly.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-02-20T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: FINLY discovery recap: p95 latency & concurrency requirements

Hi Sam / Priya —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our discovery call and the key items we captured that will help us scope a targeted evaluation with your platform team. Please correct anything I missed.

High-level goals
- Reduce visible latency for streaming-based account aggregation flows in the web app (primary UX).
- Keep p95 generation latency below 250ms on the interactive streaming path for single-turn prompts.
- Support sustained concurrency for batch and real-time use cases (see numbers below).

Current stack & constraints (what you told us)
- Frontend: React single-page app, streaming via client-side SSE.
- Backend: Python microservices behind GKE; current LLM calls proxied through an internal inference gateway to hosted vendor.
- Typical request size: 300–700 tokens (prompt + context); streaming response chunks expected every ~50–100ms for good UX.
- Current pain: spikes in p95 latency during concurrent sessions and degraded streaming chunk frequency (users see long pauses).

Quantitative targets discussed
- p95 latency target (streaming token latency): <= 250ms end-to-end for interactive flows.
- Concurrency: target sustained 120 concurrent streaming sessions for the initial rollout; peak bursts up to 350 concurrent sessions for short windows.
- Throughput: baseline batch scoring of ~5k requests/hour with 1–5s tail tolerance (non-interactive).

Success criteria for pilot
- Demonstrate p95 <= 250ms for streaming UX for a representative demo workload.
- Show stable behavior at 120 sustained concurrent streaming sessions without >5% error rate or >2x cost growth.
- Provide integration plan for prefix/KV caching and batching to reduce unit cost while preserving UX.

Open questions / assumptions
1) We assume tokenization & request shaping for streaming will be unchanged — please confirm typical chunking strategy.
2) We need access to a small sample of anonymized traces (latency + token counts) or a short replay capture to calibrate kernels.
3) Network egress and NAT timeouts: confirm any proxy timeouts or limits that might affect long-lived SSE connections.

Next steps
- Camila to run an initial microbenchmark with a representative prompt set next week (we suggested 2/24 for the technical deep-dive).
- We'll provision a short (2-week) Dedicated test lane to validate p95 and concurrency.
- You (Sam) to share architecture diagram and sample traces (see attachments/links).

Attachments: redwood-finly-discovery-notes.pdf (notes + sample prompt set)

Thanks — happy to sync live if easier.

Best,
Marissa
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.ai
From: Sam Patel <sam.patel@finly.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Priya Rao <priya@finly.com>
Date: 2027-02-20T12:35:00-08:00
Subject: Re: FINLY discovery recap: p95 latency & concurrency requirements

Hi Marissa —

Thanks for the thorough recap. That matches what we discussed. A few clarifications:
- Our 250ms p95 target is end-to-end (browser -> app -> model -> first streaming chunk visible). We measure from request send to first streamed chunk render.
- For concurrency, 120 sustained is accurate for our MVP region; global rollout could push that higher. Our current vendor shows p95 jumps during database contention and during cache misses — that's something we want to avoid.
- Attached: finly-arch-diagram.png (lightly redacted). Also dropping a link to our internal trace dump: https://drive.finly.com/traces/finly-sample-replay (we prefer short-term shared links).

One ask: can you include an expected instrumentation list (what metrics/headers to capture) so our infra team can export traces before the deep-dive?

Sam
Senior Eng Manager, Platform
Sam.Patel@finly.com
